Economics.title: Intermediate Input Prices and the Labor Share
Economics.abstract: We argue that the relative price of materials is an important determinant of the labor share of income. When materials and primary inputs are complements and the profit share is positive, a higher price of materials lowers the labor share and raises the profit share of value added, without requiring markups or returns to scale to change. We show that materials-price fluctuations align with U.S. labor-share trends, provide causal evidence on this mechanism across industries and commuting zones, and quantify its importance in a dynamic quantitative model. Finally, we use our mechanism to rationalize differential labor-share trends across countries. Economics.title: Collusion through Common Leadership
Economics.abstract: This paper studies whether common leadership, defined as two firms sharing executives or board directors, contributes to collusion. Using an explicit measure of labor market collusion from unsealed court evidence, we find that the probability of collusion between two firms increases by 11 percentage points after the onset of common leadership, a ninefold increase over the baseline rate. These results are not driven by closeness of product or labor market competition. Our findings are consistent with the increasing attention toward common leadership under Clayton Act Section 8. Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

Economics.title: From Design to Disclosure
Economics.abstract: We study the role of hard information in contractual and market settings in which the receiver can flexibly adjust allocations and transfers in response to the sender's disclosure. These settings include monopoly pricing, insurance contracting, and policy negotiations. Across these settings, the sender is worst off if she reveals her type completely because the receiver would then adjust the terms of trade to extract her surplus. Taking this feature as our central departure from the literature, we characterize the entire set of equilibrium payoffs in these disclosure games. We prove an equivalence result: a payoff profile can be approximated by an equilibrium of the disclosure game if and only if it can be achieved through information design. Thus, there exist equilibria in which the sender obtains approximately her commitment payoff.

Economics.title: Aspiring to a Better Future: Can a Simple Psychological Intervention Reduce Poverty?
Economics.abstract: Do higher aspirations for the future motivate people living in poverty to make long-term investments? Do their aspirations increase when economic conditions improve? To answer these questions, we run a 415-village field experiment with 8,300 women living in poverty in rural Kenya. We design an 80-minute workshop to help people set higher aspirations and plan to achieve them. We cross-randomise this with large unconditional cash transfers. The workshop substantially raises aspirations, labour supply, investment, revenue, and living standards 17 months later, relative to a placebo workshop. Increases in aspirations are the most likely mechanism to explain the economic effects. Cash transfers also raise aspirations, which might help to explain why transfers increase labour supply and investment. We conclude that aspirations respond to both economic and psychological interventions,…

Economics.title: Competition in Markups: A Theory of the Lerner Index in Networks and General Equilibrium
Economics.abstract: What determines demand elasticities and markups in production networks, where firms' demand and pricing are interdependent? I propose competition in markups, an equilibrium concept in which firms choose markups, taking other firms' markups as given. In partial equilibrium with vertical structures, it links upstream demand elasticities to downstream characteristics without backward induction and ties pass-through to the curvature of final demand. In general equilibrium with arbitrary industry networks, it microfounds firms' demand elasticities and markups through their within-industry market shares and four industry-level network statistics---cycle, substitution in production, substitution in consumption, and consumer-price impact. Empirical analysis of Compustat firms from 1997 to 2019 confirms the predicted variation of industry demand elasticities and firm markups. Relative to an…

Economics.title: The Welfare Effects of Price Shocks and Household Relief Packages: Evidence from an Energy Crisis
Economics.abstract: Aggregate price shocks generate unequal welfare losses both across and within income groups.Policymakers face a trade-off: price subsidies direct more support to households facing larger losses, but create inefficiencies, while transfers are less distortionary but harder to target.We develop and implement a framework to quantify this trade-off using rich panel data on households' energy spending and incomes, alongside price and policy variation from the 2022-23 European Energy Crisis.Absent policy intervention, average household welfare losses would have equalled 6% of income, with some households facing much larger losses.The combination of an energy-price subsidy and universal transfers reduced both the mean and dispersion of losses, but incurred efficiency costs equal to 12% of total relief-package revenue costs.Optimal policy entails a strictly positive price subsidy, though its…

Economics.title: Labor Market Tightness and the Reversal of Inequality Trends in Germany
Economics.abstract: Germany experienced a sharp rise in wage inequality over the two decades leading up to the Great Recession. However, a remarkable trend reversal occurred in 2010—well before the introduction of the minimum wage in 2015—when wages at the bottom of the distribution began to grow more rapidly than those higher up. This paper attributes the reversal to an increasingly tight labor market after the Great Recession, supported by strong domestic demand, and operating through several interrelated and mutually reinforcing channels. Consistent with this hypothesis, job-to-job transition rates and between-job wage growth rose markedly after the recession, especially for workers at the lower rungs of the job ladder. Concurrently, workers increasingly moved from low-paying to higher-paying firms, compressing the worker-weighted distribution of firm wage premia. Tighter labor markets also reduced…

Economics.title: The Impact of Commercial Real Estate Regulations on U.S. Output
Economics.abstract: Commercial real estate accounts for about 20% of the U.S. capital stock and is highly regulated. Yet relatively little is known about how these regulations affect economic activity or consumer welfare. This paper develops a spatial general equilibrium model of the U.S. economy with commercial real estate regulations and congestion effects, the latter providing a rationale for such regulations. The model constructs a panel of commercial real estate regulation indices for major U.S. metropolitan areas by exploiting variation in the share of parcel value attributable to land versus structures in tax assessor records compiled by Cotality. We find that a moderate relaxation of commercial real estate building regulations across U.S. cities generates large allocative efficiency gains, increasing output by 2.7% to 5.3% and welfare by 2.8% to 8.0% of lifetime consumption. We then extract the…

Economics.title: Fertility and Family Leave Policies in Germany: Optimal Policy Design in a Dynamic Framework
Economics.abstract: I develop and estimate a life-cycle discrete-choice model of fertility and female labour supply to study the optimal design of a range of child-related policies. First, I examine two German reforms that introduced wage-contingent parental leave payments and expanded access to low-cost public childcare. I find that both reforms raised completed fertility, with the parental leave reform having a particularly strong impact on highly educated women. Second, I solve for a budget-neutral optimal policy portfolio that maximizes either aggregate welfare or fertility, while ensuring that welfare and fertility do not decline for any education group. I consider four prominent child subsidies as well as the degree of tax jointness. My results show that optimal policy has the potential to increase welfare by 0.5% or fertility by 5.7%. While the solutions are qualitatively similar, they prioritize…

Economics.title: Meritocracy and Homophily in Collegial Organizations
Economics.abstract: In collegial organizations, homophily jeopardizes the recruitment of the most talented (“meritocracy”). We analyze the dynamics and welfare properties of an organization whose incumbent members coopt new ones in a forward-looking manner. We identify organizations in which meritocracy is likely to give way to favoritism and entrenchment, and investigate policy interventions (such as affirmative action, quality-based or diversity-based funding, discretionary overruling of majority decisions, blind hiring processes) and their unintended consequences.

Economics.title: Optimal Policy Rules in HANK
Economics.abstract: We characterize optimal policy rules in a business-cycle model with nominal rigidities and heterogeneous households. The policymaker has access to two instruments: the short-term nominal rate, and lump-sum transfer payments. A policymaker with a traditional dual mandate that targets aggregates uses the same policy rule as is optimal in the textbook New Keynesian model. We then consider a policymaker with a distributional objective. The optimal policy rule now contains an additional term, reflecting the effects of the policymaker’s instruments on consumption inequality. Since, in our model, monetary policy only has very limited distributional effects, this additional term does not materially change optimal monetary policy. Fiscal stimulus payments, on the other hand, have strongly progressive effects and are thus well-suited to cushion the distributional effects of cyclical fluctuations.

Why Do Union Jobs Pay More? New Evidence from Matched Employer-Employee Data
Economics.abstract: We use Canadian matched employer-employee data to assess the sources of the union pay premium. After controlling for worker heterogeneity using the two-way fixed effects approach of Abowd, Kramarz, and Margolis (AKM), we find that unionized firms pay about 15 log points more than non-unionized firms. Forty percent of this gap is linked to productivity differences between unionized and non-unionized firms as measured by value added per worker. The remaining gap reflects unions’ ability to extract more rents for workers. Our estimates imply that unions raise pay among unionized workers by around 9 log points, with considerable heterogeneity by industry and firm birth cohorts. The union effect grows to about 11 log points in an extension of the AKM approach where unions also affect the returns to unobservable worker characteristics.

Economics.title: Systemic Cyber Risk: Linking Measurement, Market Incentives, and Policy
Economics.abstract: Many firms and sectors within the global economy heavily depend on a common set of critical technology products and software services, thereby consolidating risk across a small number of potential failure points. The widespread reliance on a limited set of products and services has given rise to many single points of system vulnerability. Such concentration of risk amplifies the potential fallout from security breaches, especially since attackers have strong incentives to attack such products and services. Despite the abundance of tools available to organizations and consumers for safeguarding their data against loss or compromise, advancements in individual defense measures have been more than counterbalanced by an increased susceptibility to systemic events. In this paper, we apply economic principles to the rising danger of systemic cyber risks. The paper is organized around four…

Economics.title: In Praise of the Bayesian Bootstrap
Economics.abstract: The key takeaways from this article will be the following: (i) Anytime you can bootstrap, you should! (ii) Use the Bayesian bootstrap instead of the nonparametric bootstrap. (iii) If the bootstrap distribution looks different from the “theoretical” (usually, normal) distribution, don’t (only) report a point estimate and standard error. (iv) Instead (or in addition), report the bootstrap distribution with a plot if you have space for it or an interval if you don’t. (v) Give the Bayesian bootstrap a Bayesian interpretation. (vi) You can use a bootstrap even with (multiway) clustering.

Economics.title: Private Credit, Balance Sheets, and Financial Stability
Economics.abstract: Private credit has become an important source of business financing, raising questions about financial stability. We examine these questions using comprehensive fund- and asset-level data on private credit funds, the dominant form of private credit. Four facts emerge. First, private credit funds are primarily equity financed, with equity accounting for 65–80 percent of assets, compared with about 10 percent for US banks. Second, they engage in little maturity transformation: Fund lives span eight to twelve years, while underlying loans typically mature within two to four years. Third, portfolios are diversified across industries, geographies, and credit strategies. Fourth, equity investors have earned average net annualized returns of about 10 percent after fees, with equity cushions historically absorbing losses before creditors. These findings suggest that private credit funds do not…

Economics.title: Can Government Support for Innovation Create the Next Silicon Valley?
Economics.abstract: Can government support for innovation create the next Silicon Valley? We examine what public research and development can and cannot do to foster regional knowledge hubs. The historical record suggests that many successful hubs owe their origins partly to serendipity and favorable initial conditions. We then review causal evidence from universities, changes in intellectual property rules, new research institutions, wartime R&D, and the space race. Public R&D can raise local innovation, employment, and income, but the effects are heterogeneous, often modest relative to cost, and may partly reflect the relocation of firms and skilled workers from elsewhere. The evidence suggests a central role for complementary local inputs, including entrepreneurs, risk capital, skilled labor, firms, and institutions. Public R&D can help build a hub, but is unlikely to create one on its own.

Economics.title: The Role of Organization in Firm-Sponsored Training
Economics.abstract: Some firms are more likely than others to invest in workers’ skills. We document this phenomenon and discuss its implications in light of models of firm-sponsored skills training. The data show that better managed firms, even in the same industries and labor markets, are more likely to train, while training clusters around either managerial or frontline worker development. We argue that organizational differences provide incentives for firms to train beyond traditional explanations that focus on labor market frictions. We illustrate how organizational heterogeneity can generate training investments through a knowledge hierarchy framework where top managers with different skills build bespoke organizations tailored to their unique needs. This, in turn, makes general skill firm specific, allowing firms to capture returns on training investment.

Economics.title: Trust Violations in Research Universities
Economics.abstract: By nearly twice as much as in any other institution that Gallup tracks, public trust in research universities has fallen over the past decade. The causes are not only external. This essay examines two violations of trust that originate within the academy: research that is driven by political advocacy, and a professoriate whose range of ideological viewpoints has narrowed, especially in the humanities and social sciences. The first subordinates the pursuit of truth to political aims; the second erodes the diversity of perspectives that checks individual biases and lets research correct itself. Both break faith with the arguments originally advanced for tenure and academic freedom. Restoring trust demands a renewed commitment to disinterested inquiry and the cultivation of intellectual pluralism—objectives, both, that are best adopted voluntarily, without state censor or interference,…

Economics.title: The Role of Private Debt in the Financial Ecosystem
Economics.abstract: This paper provides an introduction to the modern private debt market and examines its rapid expansion following the 2007–2009 global financial crisis. Traditionally, economists distinguished between public debt markets and private debt in the form of bank lending. In contemporary markets, however, “private debt” refers to credit originated and held by nonbank financial intermediaries, including private credit funds and business development companies. The paper reviews the key drivers of the sector’s growth; analyzes the distinctive features of private lending arrangements and funding structures; and discusses the implications for traditional banking, financial intermediation, and financial stability. While the sector’s rapid growth and increasing complexity warrant careful monitoring, the paper argues that private debt represents an important and likely durable component of modern…

Economics.title: The Why and How of Foreign Aid
Economics.abstract: Foreign aid has become a melting pot of motivations and policies, where differently motivated actors often converge on recommended policies while the similarly motivated diverge. Breaking down the “why” and the “how” can illuminate real tensions and reveal false ones. The “why” asks which problems to tackle and who benefits: the recipient, the donor through economic, political, or soft-power returns, or everyone through global public goods. The “how” asks which strategy most cost-effectively addresses a chosen problem. Evidence is central to the “how”: Use it where it exists, produce it where it does not. In particular, approaches that improve state capacity to use and generate evidence can satisfy multiple objectives: strengthen recipient countries, benefit donors, and provide a global public good of knowledge. Ultimately, the “how” is not a linear process, but rather an iterative one…

Economics.title: The Meritocratic Consensus and Stratification in Higher Education
Economics.abstract: American colleges and universities are highly stratified by pre-college academic achievement, family background, and institutional resources. We study the meritocratic consensus in American higher education: Colleges that high-testing students (who are generally also from high-income families) attend spend dramatically more on instruction than do those that enroll lower-testing students. Stratification by test scores has been largely stable since the 1960s, but the stratification of instructional resources has risen sharply since 1970 at both private and public institutions. Nonacademic admissions criteria like athletics, legacy, and affirmative action are second-order in determining the allocation of students to universities. Potential economic justifications for the positive association of instructional expenditures with student prior achievement—q-complementarity between achievement…

Engineering and technology.title: Controlling the flow of information in optical metrology
Engineering and technology.abstract: Optical metrology has surpassed the Abbe-Rayleigh limit by leveraging nonlinear phenomena and statistical accumulation, and has recently unlocked subatomic precision using artificial intelligence estimators trained on measurand variations. Here we argue that further gains can be achieved by optimizing the flow of Fisher information carrying metrological content. We show that Fisher information flow need not follow the optical energy flow and that it exhibits resonance, diffraction and interference, singular points, and vorticity. It can exhibit a Talbot-like effect in which Fisher information density patterns repeat periodically with propagation distance, and it can be focused beyond the diffraction limit, mirroring the effect of optical superoscillation. Engineering and technology.title: Designed broken symmetries facilitate configurational complexity in nematic vortex crystals
Engineering and technology.abstract: Although widely used in modern technological applications, liquid crystals have not yet been systematically explored or utilized as reconfigurable information storage devices. Here we demonstrate that precisely designed broken symmetries in nematic vortex crystal lattices give rise to exponential configurational complexity exceeding the configurational entropy of conventional atomic crystals, and arising from the manifold ways in which surface-anchored nematic defect lines can combine to form nematic vortex crystals with distinct free-energy minima and tailored broken symmetries, thereby generalizing the interstitial and substitutional defects as well as grain boundaries in conventional crystalline materials. Engineering and technology.title: Proximal redox coupling enables oxidation damping for stable water electrolysis
Engineering and technology.abstract: The design of atomically precise catalysts requires strategies that regulate their electronic and structural dynamics under operating conditions. While conventional doping can effectively tune bulk materials, it translates poorly to single-atom catalysts (SACs), in which isolated atoms lack extended coordination and are prone to oxidative instability. Here we design atomically dispersed Ru−O−Cr motifs that enable oxidation damping during acidic oxygen evolution. In situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy shows attenuated Ru oxidation synchronized with anticorrelated and partially reversible Cr redox evolution, consistent with proximity-dependent redox coupling. This buffered redox response is accompanied by bounded and partially reversible changes in the local metal−oxygen coordination environment. Engineering and technology.title: Exploring the distributional implications of targeted residential electrification in California
Engineering and technology.abstract: The economics of residential electrification in high-cost electricity regions remain uncertain. Using metered data from over 20,000 California homes, we assess the economic, environmental, and equity impacts of end-use electrification under rollout strategies based on household income and gas infrastructure age. Even under favorable electricity rates, only 15% of households achieve positive net present values (NPVs). Cost-effectiveness improves with deeper electrification scenarios, particularly when more costs are shifted to fixed charges and for homes with existing air conditioning—54–67% of these households break even when electrifying space heating, compared to fewer than 5% of those without. Controlled flight of an insect-scale flapping-wing robot via integrated onboard sensing and computation
Engineering and technology.abstract: Aerial insects can effortlessly navigate dense vegetation, whereas similarly sized aerial robots typically depend on offboard sensors and computation to maintain stable flight. This disparity restricts insect-scale robots to operation in motion-capture environments, substantially limiting their applicability to tasks such as search-and-rescue operations and precision agriculture. In this work, we present a 1.29-gram aerial robot capable of hovering and tracking trajectories with solely onboard sensing and computation. The combination of a sensor suite, estimators, and a low-level controller achieved centimeter-scale positional flight accuracy. In addition, we developed a hierarchical controller in which a human operator provides high-level commands to direct the robot's motion. An organic semiconductor-based photocatalyst sheet for overall solar-driven water splitting
Engineering and technology.abstract: Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen using sunlight offers a route to renewable fuel, but translating this reaction into systems suitable for industrial implementation remains difficult. Photocatalyst sheets can overcome key limitations of common direct water-splitting approaches (photoelectrochemical devices and photocatalyst dispersions), but existing photocatalyst sheets rely on inorganic semiconductor nanoparticles and processing techniques that can be difficult to scale. Here we show that solution-processed organic semiconductors can form water-splitting photocatalyst sheets by simply tailoring the charge extraction layer beneath the light-absorbing film. Engineering and technology.title: A CD7-targeted AAV variant enables efficient T and NK cell engineering in vivo
Engineering and technology.abstract: Adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors have been applied for precise genome engineering in human T cells but poor tropism restricts their efficiency and translational potential. Here, through directed evolution of the AAV6 capsid in primary human T cells, we identified a family of variants containing an APR motif at residues 455-457. Engineering and technology.title: Heavy metal acrobatics: Learning dynamic control for skid-steer loaders
Engineering and technology.abstract: Automation of heavy machinery offers the opportunity to improve productivity in mechanized industries such as construction, mining, and material handling. Yet, automation of such machines is challenged by their complex dynamics, in part because of hydraulic actuation that involves fluids, flexible elements, and nonlinear delays. A concomitant challenge is the size and weight of these machines, which can make experiments on the physical systems exceedingly dangerous. Here, we show that reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation, followed by transfer of the learned policies from simulation to reality, can successfully automate acrobatic maneuvers that push a heavy construction machine to the limits of its actuation and have only previously been accomplished by a small number of elite human operators in official world-record performances. Bridging vision-language reasoning and learned control for legged navigation in the wild
Engineering and technology.abstract: Autonomous navigation in diverse real-world environments remains one of the greatest challenges in robotics. It demands both robust low-level motion control to handle diverse terrain and high-level reasoning to interpret environmental cues. We present ROAM (Robust Open-world Autonomous Mobility), a system that enables legged robots to perform kilometer-scale navigation in complex alpine and urban settings. ROAM combines the world knowledge of a vision-language model (VLM), pretrained on internet-scale data, with robust locomotion and local planning policies learned in simulation via reinforcement learning (RL). Engineering and technology.abstract: Robot acceptance is shaped by dynamic, multimodal interactions that influence trust, comfort, and behavioral intentions.

Engineering and technology.title: Autane: An autonomous crane for sustained port operations
Engineering and technology.abstract: Fully automated cranes are revolutionizing modern port operations by addressing labor shortages, improving precision, and enhancing safety. Toward this goal, we present the Autane (autonomous crane) system specifically developed for rubber tire gantry (RTG) cranes handling standardized containers in port yards, enabling autonomous safety-critical container grabbing, transport, and placement with high accuracy, adaptability, and efficiency. Autane overcomes the challenges of safe motion of large-scale cranes with centimeter-level precision requirements, providing long-distance high-precision perception. Engineering and technology.title: Environmental and material implications of global climate mitigation pathways
Engineering and technology.abstract: Reaching the goals of the Paris Agreement requires a rapid transformation of global energy systems. Yet, energy supply and use exert multiple pressures on ecosystems, human health and natural resources, raising questions about the broader environmental consequences of alternative decarbonization pathways and the resources they require. Here we analyse 24 climate mitigation pathways from three integrated assessment models using a life-cycle perspective. This enables a system-wide comparison of environmental impacts and resource requirements of global final energy provision from 2020 to 2100. Engineering and technology.title: Printing powerful soft robots on a desktop
Engineering and technology.abstract: Soft robots can achieve complex behaviors with simple control strategies. One promising approach is to embed fluidic control circuits directly into the structure of a soft robot without electronics. Automated additive manufacturing offers a route to consistently fabricate such integrated robotic systems without labor-intensive manual assembly. However, previous soft robots fabricated using this approach relied on control circuits that operated at low power, limiting their practical utility. Here, we present a 3D-printed high-power pneumatic architecture for driving soft robots. At its core is a double-expansion pneumatic oscillator inspired by the compound steam engine that converts a constant high-pressure gas input into four-phase pressure signals at high frequency. Life and practice.title: Participatory Budgeting in Public Health: Promise, Evidence, Challenges, and Opportunities
Life and practice.abstract: Participatory budgeting (PB) is a deliberative decision-making process that invites community participation to direct spending for a defined portion of public budgets. Originating in Brazil in the 1980s, PB has since diffused across the globe, including several hundred cases in the United States and Canada alone. PB programs vary but are generally characterized by five core principles: voice, vote, social inclusion, social justice, and oversight. Research on PB shows promising though moderate associations with improved population health outcomes, including infant mortality reductions and health and sanitation spending increases. Despite PB's conceptual alignment with many public health values, adoption of PB by US public health agencies remains limited, constrained by categorical funding requirements, small discretionary budgets, and a polarized sociopolitical environment. Life and practice.title: Tackling the Commercial Determinants of Obesity: A Review of Key Policies and Strategies
Life and practice.abstract: A growing body of evidence demonstrates that commercial entities play an important role in shaping the prevalence, incidence, and distribution of obesity. This narrative review examines policy solutions to address the commercial determinants of obesity. We describe how five business sectors (food, beverages, and agriculture; media and entertainment; sports and recreation; transportation; and medical care and pharmaceuticals) shape obesity prevalence through three key behavioral pathways: diet, physical activity, and use of medical care. We then examine four categories of tools available to national and subnational governments to address the commercial determinants: legal and regulatory measures, fiscal policies, market governance mechanisms, and litigation. Life and practice.title: Community Violence Impacts on Population Health
Life and practice.abstract: Community violence is a pervasive public health issue with consequences beyond injury, influencing health through physiological, psychological, and behavioral pathways. Given the growing body of research, it is an opportune time to synthesize this evidence and examine how study features shape the strength and interpretation of findings. We discuss measurement of community violence and review analytic challenges, including social selection and correlated confounders. We then evaluate evidence across four domains: health-related biomarkers, mental health and substance use, chronic diseases, and maternal and infant health. Evidence on the harms of community violence is most consistent for mental health among young people and for infant growth outcomes. Life and practice.title: Hemodynamic spectral signatures across vigilance states: a whole-night EEG/fNIRS investigation
Life and practice.abstract: Sleep is accompanied by coordinated changes in neuronal activity and cerebral hemodynamics. However, cortical hemodynamic signatures across sleep stages remain poorly characterized, partly because most human electroencephalography (EEG)/functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies are limited in duration, rarely capture deep or Rapid-Eye-Movement (REM) sleep, have low sampling rate, or rely on a sleep-deprivation paradigm, which limits the generalizability of findings. Here, we combined whole-night polysomnography, EEG and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) in healthy young adults, as a bedside technology to monitor cortical hemodynamic fluctuations. Life and practice.abstract: STUDY OBJECTIVES: Insomnia symptoms are often reported during pregnancy, prompting use of pharmacologic treatments. We explored associations between treatments used during the month before through the third month of pregnancy ("early pregnancy") and risk of birth defects using Birth Defects Study to Evaluate Pregnancy exposureS (BD-STEPS) data from 2014-2021. METHODS: Pregnancies affected by birth defects ("cases") were identified from surveillance systems in seven states; liveborn infants without birth defects ("controls") were randomly selected from the same catchment areas. Mothers of cases and controls reported early pregnancy exposures via interview, including use of prescription, over-the-counter, or herbal sleep aids. Life and practice.abstract: STUDY OBJECTIVES: Shiftworkers rarely achieve full circadian adaptation to their schedule. We studied the impact of circadian misalignment on sleep and neurobehavioral performance using a simulated shiftwork paradigm. METHODS: Nineteen individuals (mean±SD, 38±10 yrs, 10F) were studied in an 8-day inpatient protocol with a Baseline day (8h sleep), followed by an abrupt 8-hour delay shift in sleep-wake timing maintained for four days (simulated shiftwork) paired with different ambient lighting conditions to promote circadian adaptation, then a 30-hour constant routine (CR). Life and practice.title: The Wild West of Nomenclature, Definitions, and Methodologies in Rodent Sleep Scoring
Life and practice.abstract: Rodent models are essential for investigating the mechanisms and regulation of sleep, yet the field lacks a unified framework for sleep-scoring terminology, definitions, and reporting. Laboratories vary in recording modalities, temporal resolution, staging criteria, and analytical approaches, reflecting both historical practices and the diverse experimental questions addressed using rodent models. Ongoing efforts to harmonize and standardize rodent sleep methodologies are therefore important for improving rigor, reproducibility, and cross-study comparison. However, methodological harmonization also requires a shared vocabulary and clear operational definitions to understand how scoring and analytical approaches are implemented and how methodological choices influence reported outcomes. Life and practice.title: Repairing the disruption of protein homeostasis ameliorates REM sleep dysfunction in mouse models of Huntington’s disease
Life and practice.abstract: Although disruption of sleep behavior is prevalent across different neurodegenerative diseases, there is little understood about the molecular mechanisms that tie them together. To explore this relationship, we turned to the autosomal dominant disorder Huntington's disease (HD), which shares many features common to more prevalent sporadic diseases, such as abnormal protein accumulation, early cognitive changes, and cell type specific degeneration. Life and practice.abstract: STUDY OBJECTIVES: Intermittent hypoxemia is increasingly recognized as a stronger predictor of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) than the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI). We developed a sound-based AI model to detect oxygen desaturation events and estimate the oxygen desaturation index (ODI) from nocturnal breathing sounds in a fully contactless manner. Life and practice.abstract: STUDY OBJECTIVES: To assess the test-retest stability of nocturnal sleep-onset REM periods (nSOREMPs) in untreated patients with narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), and of nocturnal direct REM (nDREM) transitions and their clinical and biological correlates. Life and practice.title: Labor Unions and Better Health
Life and practice.abstract: Social-class inequities in health arise from power imbalances in our political-economic system. However, through labor-union organizing, workers can build power to improve their life chances and health. In our review, we describe the rich historical, theoretical, and mechanistic evidence linking unions and health and critically evaluate the state of quantitative research on the topic. Most individual-level and ecological studies have estimated small beneficial or null union-health associations. However, as we describe, the studies are limited in number, particularly outside the Global North, and face many technical and conceptual challenges, including feedback loops between unions and societies' political-economic contexts. We conclude with recommendations for enhancing the rigor and utility of union-health research, including by richly contextualizing studies' findings and by…

Life and practice.title: Respiratory self-similarity is a sleep apnea endotype that predicts cardiovascular disease related mortality
Life and practice.abstract: STUDY OBJECTIVES: Pathological respiratory chemoreflex activation (high loop gain) in sleep apnea may activate the carotid body and induce excessive sympathetic nerve output, and independently add to the risk of adverse outcomes. This study aims to determine whether a high loop gain of the respiratory control system during sleep, estimated by respiratory self-similarity (SS) and the algorithm-derived central respiratory event index (CREI), is associated with new-onset cardiovascular disease (CVD) and CVD-related mortality. METHODS: A secondary analysis of The Sleep Heart Health Study (SHHS) and Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA). High SS% and CREI were defined as the highest quartile. Life and practice.abstract: Background A higher dietary protein intake is often advocated to preserve fat-free mass during energy restriction-induced weight loss, yet the magnitude of effect in previous meta-analyses is highly variable. Objectives We aimed to determine the effects of a higher dietary protein intake on body composition during energy restriction-induced weight loss in individuals with overweight or obesity, with consideration for exercise, age, and protein difference. Subgroup meta-analysis and meta-regression were performed to…

Life and practice.abstract: BACKGROUND: Rapid social progress has transformed the health profile of Chinese children and adolescents, with declining diseases associated with poverty and rising diseases associated with wealth. This study aims to describe national trends in disease transitions and examine their associations with multidimensional provincial development. METHODS: In this retrospective study, we analysed data from the 2000, 2005, 2010, 2014, and 2019 waves of the nationwide, repeated, cross-sectional Chinese National Surveys on Students' Constitution and Health in Han Chinese children and adolescents aged 7-18 years from 30 provinces in mainland China. Life and practice.title: Nutrition in abrupt sunlight reduction scenarios: a scenario-based modeling study of malnutrition prevention in low-income regions
Life and practice.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
Life and practice.abstract: Background Abrupt sunlight reduction scenarios (ASRSs), triggered by nuclear war, volcanic eruption, or asteroid strike, risk global agricultural collapse. Despite resilient food interventions, economic inequality may leave low-income countries (LICs) at severe risk of malnutrition even where global food production is partially maintained. Objectives To assess the nutritional adequacy of low-cost ASRS-resilient food baskets (~$1/person/d) for LIC populations across 2 postdisaster periods, and to identify micronutrient gaps requiring targeted intervention. Methods A scenario-based nutritional modeling study was conducted. Food baskets were constructed for 2 periods: Period 1 (≤1 y postdisaster), based on conventional crop stocks and offal, and Period 2 (years 2–3), incorporating single-cell protein, lignocellulosic sugar, seaweed, and wheat flour. Life and practice.title: Impact of supplementation with fortified balanced energy–protein during pregnancy on birth outcomes: a community-based randomized trial among pregnant females in southern Nepal
Life and practice.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
Life and practice.abstract: Background The World Health Organization recommends balanced energy–protein (BEP) dietary supplementation in undernourished populations to reduce risk of stillbirth and small-for-gestational age (SGA), but variation in the composition of interventions has hindered scientific consensus. Objectives To assess the effect of daily fortified BEP supplementation during pregnancy on SGA birth and secondary birth outcomes. Life and practice.title: (R)-1,3-butanediol (S)-lactate ester improves insulin sensitivity, modulates appetite hormones, and reduces urea excretion: a randomized controlled crossover trial in adults with obesity
Life and practice.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition

The molecule (R)-1,3-butanediol (S)-lactate ester (LaKe) is a new supplement that offers dual supplementation of lactate and βHB. Objectives This study aims to evaluate whether 28 d of LaKe supplementation followed by acute dosing would 1 ) improve insulin sensitivity and 2 ) influence appetite-regulating hormones, gastric emptying, substrate metabolism, and body weight. Life and practice.title: Riboflavin status in pregnancy and its association with hemoglobin and anemia risk: cross-sectional findings from the OptiPREG study
Life and practice.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
Life and practice.abstract: Background Anemia in pregnancy poses a serious health problem for females globally. In addition to iron deficiency, the most common nutritional cause of anemia, a deficiency of riboflavin (required for iron metabolism) may also be implicated, but this has rarely been investigated. Objectives This study investigated the association of riboflavin status with hemoglobin (Hb) concentrations and anemia risk during pregnancy. Business.abstract: In this ethnographic study, we develop the concept of temporal riskwork -- actions taken to alter the temporal dynamics of risk -- by examining how riskworkers navigated situations of multiple dynamically evolving risks under severe time constraints. In such contexts, decisions about how and when to act are critically interdependent and made with attention to assessing urgencies, priorities and volatility of risk. Our study revealed how risk can present both synchronic and diachronic competing temporal demands, requiring temporally complex riskwork. We studied a mental health crisis team where actors collectively responded to clients’ urgent, often accelerating risks in high-stakes, time-pressured environments. Business.title: Private debt versus bank debt in corporate borrowing
Business.abstract: Using administrative bank loan-level data matched to private debt deals, we study the interaction between private and bank debt for a large segment of dual borrowers. These firms use private debt for investment and bank credit lines for liquidity insurance. Private debt carries higher spreads and commonly features flexible, equity-like terms that are associated with greater reliance on bank credit lines. Relative to bank-only borrowers, dual borrowers obtain more and larger credit lines and draw them more intensively following liquidity shocks. Our findings suggest that private debt substitutes for bank term loans but complements banks’ provision of credit lines.

Business.title: The Asymmetry in Responsible Investing Preferences and Beliefs
Business.abstract: Empirical stylized facts in the literature concerning “sin” versus “angel” stocks display marked asymmetries in investor behavior. Through a set of experiments, we examine whether such biases can be micro-founded via individuals’ preferences and belief formations. With respect to portfolio allocation decisions, we find that the responses to negative environmental and social externalities are several times larger in magnitude than their responses to comparable positive externalities, ceteris paribus. Negative externalities also modestly increase pessimism about future investment performance, whereas positive externalities have little discernible effect on beliefs. This asymmetry is pervasive across our sample, exhibits heterogeneity across individuals, and is comparable to or greater in magnitude than estimates observed in loss aversion analyses. Business.title: Biodiversity Risk in the Corporate Bond Market
Business.abstract: We show that a biodiversity risk premium has emerged in the U.S. corporate bond market following the United Nations Biodiversity Conference (COP15) in October 2021. COP15 placed biodiversity on the global regulatory agenda and raised transition risks for exposed firms. After COP15, a one standard deviation increase in a firm’s biodiversity footprint is associated with a 7% increase in its secondary market yield spreads, whereas this relation is insignificant before COP15. The biodiversity effect is also present in primary bond markets, most pronounced for medium-term bonds and distinct from climate-related mechanisms. Furthermore, a higher biodiversity footprint is associated with a lower likelihood of issuing medium-term bonds after COP15, consistent with firms managing their biodiversity-related risks. Business.title: What’s at Stake? Understanding the Role of Home Equity in Flood Insurance Demand
Business.abstract: Changing flood insurance demand shifts climate risk across homeowners, lenders, and governments. We show that flood insurance take-up follows rising and falling home equity over the housing boom and bust across markets with different price dynamics. To isolate the causal effect of risk shifting on insurance demand, we study flood insurance policy renewals over the housing bust, exploiting granular differences in purchase timing that led policyholders to experience differential changes in skin-in-the-game exposure to flood risk for the same change in home equity. When homeowners have less equity exposure to flood losses, they are less likely to renew their policies. Business.title: Rethinking Distribution Shifts: Empirical Analysis and Modeling for Tabular Data
Business.abstract: Different distribution shifts require different interventions, and algorithms must be grounded in the specific shifts they address. However, methodological development for robust algorithms typically relies on structural assumptions that lack empirical validation. Advocating for an empirically grounded data-driven approach to algorithm development, we build an empirical testbed comprising natural shifts across 8 tabular data sets, 172 distribution pairs over 45 methods, and 90,000 method configurations encompassing empirical risk minimization and distributionally robust optimization (DRO) methods. We find that Y|X-shifts are most prevalent in our testbed, in stark contrast to the heavy focus on X (covariate)-shifts in the machine learning literature, and that the performance of robust algorithms is no better than that of vanilla methods. Business.title: The Data-Driven Censored Newsvendor Problem
Business.abstract: We study a censored variant of the data-driven newsvendor problem, where the decision maker must select an ordering quantity that minimizes expected overage and underage costs based only on offline censored sales data rather than historical demand realizations. Our goal is to understand how the degree of historical demand censoring affects the performance of any learning algorithm for this problem. To isolate this impact, we adopt a distributionally robust optimization framework, evaluating policies according to their worst-case regret over an ambiguity set of distributions. This set is defined by the largest historical order quantity (the observable boundary of the data set), and contains all distributions matching the true demand distribution up to this boundary while allowing them to be arbitrary afterward. Business.title: Benefiting from Culture Wars: Resource Mobilization in Polarized Issue Domains
Business.abstract: Organizations engaging with contested social issues may struggle to mobilize resources due to disapproval from hostile audiences. Yet, some may benefit from increased support from sympathetic audiences, leaving unclear when such support will outweigh opposition. We propose that variation in audience reactions depends partly on how contestation is structured. We theorize that ideological polarization—the extent to which opposing stances on an issue sort along ideological lines—may enhance resource mobilization in contested issue domains. As polarization increases, contested issues pit opposing identities against each other and heighten threats to sympathetic audiences’ worldviews. Business.title: The Consequences of Pay Standing under Pay Range Transparency
Business.abstract: Pay range transparency—that is, disclosing the minimum and maximum pay for a job rather than individuals’ actual pay—has become the most prevalent form of pay transparency. Yet, existing theories explain employee reactions to pay information through present-focused, interpersonal comparisons with coworkers’ pay. We theorize that pay range transparency instead directs employees to interpret their structural pay standing—their pay position relative to the disclosed range boundaries—as a forward-looking signal of the organization’s recognition and structural room for pay growth. Business.title: Deadly Disease, Fear, and Ostracism in the Credit Market
Business.abstract: This paper exploits the 2014 U.S. Ebola outbreak as a natural experiment to examine how fear distorts mortgage credit allocation. We find a 3.8-percentage-point increase in mortgage denial rates for Black applicants during the outbreak, despite negligible infection risk. Approved Black borrowers have stronger credit profiles and lower default rates, yet are less likely to receive loan modifications when delinquent. These effects are absent in algorithm-driven FinTech lending and reverse quickly postoutbreak—patterns inconsistent with statistical discrimination. Robustness tests rule out alternative explanations related to political cycles, labor market impacts, applicant pool composition changes, and bank financial conditions. Business.title: Do Fund Managers’ Commitments to Responsible Investing Affect Private Information Acquisition, Information Environment, and Corporate Sustainability?
Business.abstract: We investigate the effects of mutual funds’ commitments to responsible investing on their information acquisition activities and the corresponding externalities for other stakeholders. After committing to responsible investing (via United Nations Principles for Responsible Investment (UNPRI)), fund managers increase private information acquisition activities, that is, corporate site visits, particularly focusing on environmental and social issues. These visits generate negligible private investment value for the visiting funds. Business.title: Corporate Contributions to Ballot Measure Campaigns: Real Effects and Valuation
Business.abstract: We analyze novel data on corporate contributions to ballot initiatives at the U.S. state level. Firms make large contributions to ballot measure campaigns in favor of or against specific initiatives. They contribute significantly more to business initiatives compared with ideological initiatives. Corporate campaign spending is systematically associated with the likelihood that a ballot measure passes. Contributing firms experience changes in sales growth following the passage of important ballot measures. Following successful (failed) initiatives, all firms in affected industries exhibit significantly more positive (negative) cumulative abnormal returns around the election, but contributing firms do more so than peers. Business.title: Banking on a Corporate Rebrand
Business.abstract: Firms often rebrand to counter negative shocks, but can it work? Using a historical natural experiment, we analyze a large sample of companies from the same industry (banking) that shared very similar names, but overwhelmingly decided to change them in response to a common, negative news shock. U.S. entry into World War I in 1917 created a sudden anti-German backlash against anything that invoked an association with the now enemy. After 1917, the few German-named banks that kept their tainted names saw significant declines in assets, deposits, and market share relative to other banks. Business.title: Opinion Trumps Fact: Entry and Competition in Online Political News
Business.abstract: This paper examines how new entrants influenced content strategies in the U.S. online political news business from 2014 to 2021. Using a novel measure of article opinionation that captures the extent to which an article displays editorializing and persuasive language, we provide correlational evidence that new entrants produce articles that are more opinionated than those of incumbents, even when reporting on the same event. We then show that there is an economic rationale for this content strategy: opinionated articles receive more engagement on Twitter, and this engagement translates to increased webpage visits, crucial for advertising revenue. Business.title: Silent female representation and tech entrepreneurial project evaluation: The role of evaluators' genders
Business.abstract: Research Summary We examine how the nature of female representation in tech entrepreneurial projects may be related to the evaluations of the projects. We argue that silent female representation —i.e., women are present but do not speak in representing projects—may reinforce the stereotyped view of women, resulting in lower project evaluations relative to male‐only projects, whereas active female representation may not lead to evaluation penalty. We further predict that the negative association between silent female representation and project evaluation is stronger when the evaluators are women than when they are men. Business.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Sales Productivity: Field Experiments in Online Retail
Business.abstract: We quantify the short-term impact of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) on sales performance through a series of large-scale randomized field experiments involving millions of users and products at a leading crossborder online retail platform. Business.title: Shadow banks on the rise: Evidence across market segments
Business.abstract: This paper examines the comparative advantages of shadow banks across market segments. Combining credit bureau data on retail loans in India with weather shocks as a proxy for credit demand, we show that Fintechs respond more in uncollateralized markets. In contrast, non-Fintech shadow banks exhibit stronger responsiveness in collateralized markets. Exploiting geographic heterogeneity in the adoption of digital payments, we identify technology as the key advantage for Fintechs. Leveraging four natural experiments, we document the significance of lower regulation for non-Fintech shadow banks. Our results suggest that the comparative advantage of shadow banks differs across market segments.

Business.title: Is Informed Short Selling Concentrated in Family Firms? Evidence from a Reinvestigation
Business.abstract: We reinvestigate Anderson, Reeb, and Zhao's findings that informed short selling is unique to family firms and driven by information leakage from internal disputes. Using the same firm sample and more comprehensive short‐selling data, we find that short selling predicts future returns in both family and nonfamily firms. We also find no significant difference in abnormal short selling before negative earnings announcements. In extended sample periods, short selling continues to predict returns for nonfamily firms under both ownership‐based and familial‐link definitions. Overall, our evidence suggests that short sellers are broadly informed and that family firms are not uniquely vulnerable.

Business.title: The role of financial markets in the unraveling of credit
Business.abstract: We investigate how long an insolvent debtor can avoid default when survival benefits creditors collectively, but individual creditors gain from early repayment. Standard theory predicts that debt is not rolled over and default is immediate. Previous experimental studies of related environments suggest that liquidation is delayed, and we confirm that pattern here. We then study how secondary markets affect outcomes. The duration of the credit pool is unaffected, but average net payoffs increase because claims are held longer before redemption. With markets, realized payoff dispersion is significantly higher. Prices do not predict liquidation timing but correlate with realized payoffs.

Business.title: Comparing Factor Models Under Regime Switching
Business.abstract: We compare factor pricing models using the “test-asset irrelevance” result but under regime switching. We show that the unconditional squared Sharpe ratio measure is no longer appropriate for model comparison when returns are subject to regime shifts. Business.title: Looking the Part? How Candidates’ Race and Attire Shape Employers’ Hiring Decisions in a Low-Wage Labor Market
Business.abstract: Racial disparities in employment persist in the United States, particularly in low-wage labor markets in which employers frequently cite self-presentation, especially attire, as a basis for hiring decisions. Yet, whether improving professional attire yields equal returns across racial groups remains largely unexamined. Drawing on status characteristics theory, we argue that professional attire functions as an ambiguous proxy for unobservable traits such as motivation and reliability, making it susceptible to racialized interpretations. We predict that professional attire will yield weaker hiring returns for Black candidates than for their White counterparts and that perceived professionalism mediates this gap. Business.title: The Economics of Waste Valorization
Business.abstract: As the spread of waste imposes substantial environmental and economic burdens, a newer operational strategy, waste valorization, is gaining attention. This approach transforms production-generated byproduct waste into valuable, distinct products, creating intricate production and demand interdependencies that traditional strategies like remanufacturing and coproduction cannot fully capture. In this study, we examine the impacts of these interdependencies within a two-stage stochastic production decision model to determine optimal production quantities under waste valorization. Our findings reveal that a higher waste valorization rate does not always benefit the manufacturer, especially if the waste incurs disposal costs. Computer science.abstract: In classical mathematics, ordinal arithmetic is well-studied; constructively, addition and multiplication are well-known. We study constructive ordinal exponentiation, where ordinals are taken to be transitive, extensional, and wellfounded orders on sets. Computer science.title: The commutativity problem for effective varieties of formal series, and applications
Computer science.journal: Journal of the ACM
Computer science.abstract: A formal series in noncommuting variables Σ over the rationals is a mapping Σ * → Q from the free monoid generated by Σ to the rationals. We say that it is commutative if the output does not depend on the order of the symbols in the input. The commutativity problem for a class of series takes as input a (finite presentation of) a series from the class and amounts to establishing whether it is commutative. Computer science.title: Person Recognition at Altitude and Range: Fusion of Face, Body Shape and Gait
Computer science.journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
Computer science.abstract: We address the problem of whole-body person recognition in unconstrained environments. This problem arises in surveillance scenarios such as those in the IARPA Biometric Recognition and Identification at Altitude and Range (BRIAR) program, where biometric data is captured at long standoff distances, elevated viewing angles, and under adverse atmospheric conditions (e.g., turbulence and high wind velocity). Computer science.title: Optimal Inapproximability of Satisfiable k-LIN over Non-Abelian Groups
Computer science.journal: Journal of the ACM
Computer science.abstract: A seminal result of Håstad [19] shows that for k ≥ 3, it is NP-hard to find an assignment that satisfies 1/|G|+ε fraction of the constraints of a given k -LIN instance over an abelian group, even if there is an assignment that satisfies (1 − ε) fraction of the constraints, for any constant ε > 0. Engebretsen, Holmerin, and Russell [14] later showed that the same hardness result holds for k -LIN instances over any finite non-abelian group. Unlike the abelian case, where we can efficiently find a solution if the instance is satisfiable, in the non-abelian case, it is NP-complete to decide if a given system of linear equations is satisfiable or not, as shown by Goldmann and Russell [16]. Surprisingly, for certain non-abelian groups G , given a satisfiable k -LIN instance over G , one can in fact do better than just outputting a random assignment using a simple but clever algorithm. Computer science.title: Enhancing Gradient Inversion Attacks in Federated Learning via Hierarchical Feature Optimization
Computer science.journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
Computer science.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a compelling paradigm for privacy-preserving distributed machine learning, allowing multiple clients to collaboratively train a global model by transmitting locally computed gradients to a central server without exposing their private data. Nonetheless, recent studies find that the gradients exchanged in the FL system are also vulnerable to privacy leakage, e.g., an attacker can invert shared gradients to reconstruct sensitive data by leveraging pre-trained generative adversarial networks (GAN) as prior knowledge. However, existing attacks simply perform gradient inversion in the latent space of the GAN model, which limits their expression ability and generalizability. To tackle these challenges, we propose Gradient Inversion over Feature Domains (GIFD), which disassembles the GAN model and searches the hierarchical features of the intermediate…

Computer science.title: Burst Spiking Neural Networks
Computer science.journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
Computer science.abstract: A central goal of current Spiking Neural Network (SNN) research is to improve their accuracy toward becoming low-power alternatives to Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). This work further argues that realizing this ambition requires improving not only accuracy but also robustness, defined as the ability to maintain correct predictions under input perturbations. We identify two key issues in existing SNN methods that undermine robustness. First, binary spiking activations can produce large activation-state changes under small perturbations. Second, the lack of effective weight constraints makes network outputs more sensitive to input variations. To this end, we propose Burst Spiking Neural Networks (BuSNNs), built upon Burst-enhanced Spiking Neurons (BSNs) and a Dynamic Weight Constraint (DWC) mechanism. BSNs incorporate burst firing to provide a graded spiking pattern. This spiking…

Computer science.title: Representation of Directed Acyclic Graphs by Sequences of Instructions for Symbolic Regression
Computer science.journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
Computer science.abstract: Symbolic Regression (SR) aims to discover a closed-form mathematical expression that fits an observed dataset by representing those expressions as Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). A DAG with k internal nodes admits Θ(k!) equivalent node orderings of the same expression, so structurally identical candidates repeatedly reach the fitness evaluator of the solver model, consuming search budget. We introduce ISALSR (Instruction Set and Language for Symbolic Regression), an encoding that maps every labeled DAG to a canonical string over a two-tier alphabet of structural and operation-labeled tokens. Canonical strings are reached via a greedy algorithm guided by 1-Weisfeiler-Leman (1-WL) subtree hashing. We prove that the canonical string is a complete labeled-DAG invariant under a reachability condition: two expressions share their string if and only if their DAGs are isomorphic. ISALSR…

Computer science.title: Vector Map as Language: Toward Unified Remote Sensing Vector Mapping
Computer science.journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
Computer science.abstract: Remote sensing vector mapping aims to generate structured maps of geospatial entities, such as buildings, roads, and water bodies, from remote sensing imagery. In practice, vector maps usually contain multiple category layers and heterogeneous entity structures, requiring a unified model for diverse mapping needs. However, existing methods typically represent vector objects as polygons or graphs, making them suitable only for specific categories: polygons poorly capture topological relations, while graphs often blur instance boundaries. We observe that language, as a natural medium for human communication, offers a flexible and expressive representation that can accommodate heterogeneous map elements, including geometry, semantics, and topology. Motivated by this insight, we propose Vector Map as Language (VecLang), a unified paradigm that reformulates multiclass vector mapping as…

Computer science.title: TimeSeek: Multi-Task and Multi-Domain Pretraining for Generalized Time Series Analytics
Computer science.journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
Computer science.abstract: Time series analytics has been widely applied across various domains. While existing time series foundation models (TSFMs) have demonstrated promising results, they still face two major challenges: 1) Most TSFMs mainly rely on stacking Transformer layers to increase parameter size, lacking the ability to adaptively model complex time series patterns from multi-domain data. 2) Current TSFMs are primarily pre-trained for specific tasks, e.g., forecasting or anomaly detection, and a few models support multiple tasks, but they fail to fully leverage task specificity and commonality, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address these challenges, we propose TimeSeek, a novel generalized time series analytics model that adaptively models time series patterns from multi-domain data and unifies multiple tasks in pre-training. Conceptually, TimeSeek is guided by selective information sharing…

Computer science.title: Contextual Chamfer Distance for Point Cloud Restoration
Computer science.journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
Computer science.abstract: Accurate similarity measurement between point clouds is crucial for 3D geometry restoration. Chamfer Distance (CD) and its variants quantify such similarity in a permutation-invariant manner, yet they emphasize low-order point-wise proximity, leading to clustered distributions and long-range structural distortions that undermine geometric fidelity. This work rethinks point cloud similarity from a high-order standpoint and introduces Contextual Chamfer Distance (CCD), a geometrically consistent formulation that jointly models point-wise proximity, local distribution consistency, and long-range structural consistency. Specifically, Patch Density Consistency (PDC) aligns relative patch densities between predicted and ground-truth points, promoting spatial coverage for geometric completeness, while Anchor Normal Consistency (ANC) models long-range relationships through anchor normals…

Computer science.title: Bridging the Thermal Gap: Data-Model Collaborative Transfer for Infrared Perception
Computer science.journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
Computer science.abstract: Infrared visual perception fundamentally differs from visible-domain vision due to its distinct thermal imaging mechanism and varying imaging conditions. Existing methods typically decouple data construction from model transfer, overlooking their interdependence: model accuracy and robustness depend critically on the coverage and composition of training observations, while effective model transfer requires explicit modeling of infrared-specific imaging characteristics. To address this issue, we propose a data-model collaborative transfer framework for infrared visual perception. At the data level, a task-responsive generator learns weights over a feasible infrared imaging-variation space to construct informative training observations. At the model level, a formation-guided representation module derives complementary radiance-structure and response-detail descriptors from infrared…

Computer science.title: Generative Point Cloud Registration With Match-ControlNet
Computer science.journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
Computer science.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel 3D registration paradigm, Generative Point Cloud Registration, which bridges advanced 2D generative models with 3D matching tasks to enhance registration performance. Our key idea is to generate cross-view consistent image pairs that are well-aligned with the source and target point clouds, enabling geometry-color feature fusion to facilitate robust matching. To ensure high-quality matching, the generated image pair should feature both 2D-3D geometric consistency and cross-view texture consistency. To this end, we introduce DepthMatch-ControlNet and LiDARMatch-ControlNet, two matching-specific, controllable 2D generative models. Specifically, for depth camera-based 3D registration with point clouds derived from the depth maps, DepthMatch-ControlNet leverages the depth-conditioned generation capabilities of ControlNet to synthesize perspective-view RGB…

Computer science.title: Synergizing LLMs and Formal Methods for Neural-Symbolic Reasoning
Computer science.journal: Communications of the ACM
Computer science.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in natural language understanding, generation, and reasoning, but their outputs remain probabilistic and error-prone. Formal methods (FM), by contrast, provide mathematically rigorous reasoning, but suffer from limited accessibility. This article explores a neural-symbolic paradigm that unifies these complementary strengths and presents case studies that illustrate how LLMs can lower the entry barrier to formal methods while the latter provide reliability, interpretability, and guarantees absent in purely neural AI models. We argue that synergizing LLMs with formal methods is a promising direction for building AI systems that are not only powerful but also trustworthy by construction.

Computer science.title: Image Quality Assessment for Machine-oriented Communication
Computer science.journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
Computer science.abstract: The rapid development of Multimoal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has driven the evolution of communication paradigms, making the transmission of visual information in extremely low-bandwidth possible. However, as it is oriented toward computer vision tasks rather than humans, there is no widely accepted metric for its evaluation. To address this issue, we conduct a comprehensive visual quality assessment of machine oriented communication systems. Specifically, we (1) at the source level: a generative codec framework is established, with a MLLM communication pipeline through cross-modal generation between images and text. (2) at the channel level: images are transmitted using channel encoding/decoding strategies in different physical environments, and construct a dataset with 12k pairs of reference/distorted images. (3) at the sink level: 50 computer vision models are implemented to…

Computer science.title: A Simple but Efficient Method to Achieve High Performance with Extreme Sparsity
Computer science.journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
Computer science.abstract: Pruning effectively removes redundant parameters and computations from neural networks, reduces model storage space, and saves time, memory, and energy during the training and inference phases. However, current pruning methods perform well at moderate and high sparsity, but the performance difference with dense network models at extreme sparsity is huge. In order to bridge the accuracy gap between extremely sparse and dense models, this paper proposes a simple but efficient pruning strategy-Tensor Decomposition Based Iterative Magnitude Pruning (TDIMP) method. This strategy uses tensor theory to optimize the model structure before IMP to reduce the search space of the sparse subnetwork during pruning, thus improving the hit rate of the optimal sparse subnetwork. Specifically, firstly, the weight matrix or weight tensor of the dense model is represented as a low-rank tensor…

Computer science.title: Urban Architect: Steerable 3D Driving Scene Generation With Layout Prior
Computer science.journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
Computer science.abstract: Text-to-3D generation has achieved remarkable success via large-scale text-to-image diffusion models. Nevertheless, scaling this methodology to large-scale driving scenes is underexplored. Driving scenes, characterized by numerous elements, intricate arrangement relationships, and vast scale, present a formidable barrier to the interpretability of ambiguous textual descriptions for effective model optimization. In this work, we surmount the limitations by introducing a compositional 3D layout representation into text-to-3D paradigm, serving as an additional prior. It comprises a set of semantic primitives with simple geometric structures and explicit arrangement relationships, complementing textual descriptions and enabling steerable generation. Specifically, we represent the scene via 2D Gaussian splatting and develop two innovative optimization strategies: (1) Layout-Guided…

Computer science.title: 2D Gaussian Splatting for Semantic Segmentation via Discrete-to-Continuous Representation toward Boundary-Preserving Feature Upsampling
Computer science.journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
Computer science.abstract: High-quality semantic segmentation requires not only rich semantic understanding but also precise delineation of object boundaries. While prevailing methods rely on discrete feature representations that often lead to boundary misalignment, jagged contours, and blurry edges along complex contours, we present GSSeg, a novel semantic segmentation paradigm based on Gaussian Splatting that has been successfully applied to 3D scene reconstruction. Specifically, GSSeg reformulates the discrete feature space as continuous Gaussian fields, thereby rendering spatial continuity modeling to produce high-quality segmentation results. However, directly adapting 2DGS to existing pipelines suffers from the structural granularity loss in low-resolution features and the inherent low-pass limitations of Gaussian rendering. To address the insufficient structural granularity available for…

Computer science.title: DepthGS: Depth-Guided Gaussian Splatting with Adaptive Regularization for High-Quality Surface Reconstruction
Computer science.journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
Computer science.abstract: Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as an efficient representation for novel view synthesis, offering fast differentiable rendering and high visual fidelity, and has increasingly been extended to surface reconstruction. However, the relationship between depth information and reconstruction error remains insufficiently understood, limiting the principled design of geometric optimization strategies. To address this issue, we propose DepthGS, a depth-guided Gaussian splatting framework. We derive theoretical relations between depth discrepancies and reconstruction error under single-view and multi-view conditions. For single-view optimization, we propose a depth-difference-guided adaptive normal regularization strategy that modulates the normal constraint strength using a geometric reliability weight computed from local depth differences. Computer science.title: Revisiting Overestimation Bias of Q-learning: Breaking Bias Propagation Chains Does Well
Computer science.journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
Computer science.abstract: This paper revisits the overestimation bias of Q-learning from a new perspective, i.e., the breaking bias propagation chains. We make five-fold contributions. First, we analyze the estimation bias propagation chains of Q-learning, and find that the bias propagated from previous steps dominates the maximum Q-value estimation bias and slows the convergence speed, instead of the current bias. Second, we propose a novel positive-negative bias alternating algorithm called Alternating Q-learning (AQ). It breaks the unidirectional estimation bias propagation chains via alternately executing Q-learning and Double Q-learning. We show theoretically that there exist suitable alternating parameters to eliminate the propagation bias.
